~/Documents/School/Lang/quiet_shift_arti.content:
THE QUIET SHIFT (article excerpt)
When the new bus line opened on Alder Street in March, the city expected riders to fill it within a year. Instead, the route became a quiet place to read. Commuters who once drove now sit with books and phones, and small businesses along the line report more morning customers. Planners call this a side effect of reliable transit: people trust the bus enough to stop checking the clock. The author argues that cities should measure success not only by ridership but by how many people spend transit time on something they chose. Critics say the data is thin: the study surveyed only 212 riders on two weekday mornings. Still, the author concludes that the quiet shift matters because it changes how people feel about shared public space.

https://civics-library.test/cases/greer-.title: Greer v. Port Alder Board (1971): case summary
https://civics-library.test/cases/greer-.content: Decided March 15, 1971. Vote: 6-3. Holding: a municipal board may not deny a transit operator a permit using standards it never published; due process requires that agencies state the criteria they apply. Opinion of the Court by Justice Ellery. Dissent: Justices Dane and Orr, who argued the board's discretion was within its legal authority. Significance: an early application of procedural due process to local transit permits.

https://civics-quiz.test/greer-case-summ.title: Greer v Port Alder summary (study guide)
https://civics-quiz.test/greer-case-summ.content: Greer v. Port Alder Board was decided in 1961. The Court ruled 5-4 for the board, upholding its permit system. Often confused with a 1971 zoning case.
